analysis.one_liner: Caps carbon emissions and pays the auction proceeds to every American as a quarterly dividend.
analysis.headline: A carbon cap-and-dividend bill introduced with no cosponsors 18 days before Congress ended; it was referred to two House committees and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap how much oil, coal, and natural gas can be sold in the U.S. each year, shrinking the cap until 2050. Fossil fuel producers and importers would have to buy permits at quarterly auctions, starting at $40 per ton and rising yearly. All auction money would go into a trust fund and be paid out equally, tax-free, every quarter to lawful residents with a Social Security number. The bill also adds fees on carbon-intensive imports to keep foreign factories from undercutting U.S. producers, and includes air-pollution monitoring for communities near fossil fuel facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly every lawful U.S. resident: each eligible individual would receive an equal, tax-free quarterly share of all auction proceeds, and the emissions cap targets the climate and air pollution that affect everyone. Communities near fossil fuel facilities gain monitoring and enforcement of co-pollutant reductions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Lawful U.S. residents with an SSN

how_it_helps.text: All proceeds from the carbon permit auctions go to a Healthy Climate Trust Fund and are paid out as equal, pro rata quarterly dividends to every eligible individual, and the dividends are excluded from gross income (not taxed).

The cap starts 15% below 2015 U.S. emissions in 2025, reaches 50% below by 2030, and 90% below by 2050, with reports required if targets must be tightened to reach net zero or avert catastrophic climate impacts.

The bill directs air quality monitoring in frontline communities and authorizes additional EPA measures if co-pollutant emissions affecting those communities do not fall as fast as the carbon targets.

Border adjustment fees on carbon-intensive imports (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, and more) match the cost domestic producers pay for permits, and U.S. exporters receive offsetting payments, so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut by countries without carbon rules.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, coal mines, and fuel importers, who must buy a shrinking supply of permits for every ton they sell and face triple the market price as a penalty for missing surrender deadlines. Part of those costs would be passed through to consumer prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, offset for most households by the dividend.

drawbacks.text: Permit costs would raise prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, and although the dividend offsets the increase for most households, some households could see higher costs while waiting for the quarterly payment.
Dividends require a valid Social Security number and lawful presence, so some residents would face higher fuel prices without receiving the payment.

The border fee and export rebate system depends on the Treasury defining comparable goods and foreign 'equivalent measures,' and could invite trade disputes until international agreements take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households, the dividend would offset the fuel price increases the cap creates, and the design deliberately limits hoarding and speculation in permits. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers and, through prices, partly on consumers, so the plan's fairness hinges on the dividend being paid reliably and promptly each quarter. Overall the benefits are broad and the costs concentrated, which is also why the bill faced no traction in a fossil-fuel-heavy Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and sat there until Congress ended 18 days after introduction, never reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer introduced the bill on December 16, 2024, 18 days before the 118th Congress ended.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees; neither took action, and no markup, hearing, floor vote, or Senate action appears in the record before the session ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers avoided a permit requirement and rising per-ton prices, and consumers avoided the near-term pass-through to fuel and power prices, while the emissions cap, the dividends, and the air-pollution monitoring never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Donald S. Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to two committees.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor; climate legislation in this Congress generally split by party.

industries.industry: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: They would have to buy a shrinking annual supply of permits for every ton of fuel sold, with a starting floor of $40 per ton rising $10 yearly and triple-price penalties for noncompliance. Their interest in killing the bill ran against the dividend and emissions reductions that benefit the public.
A shrinking fossil fuel cap with rising permit prices makes clean energy relatively cheaper, speeding the transition without a regulatory alternative the industry chooses.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: They bear higher input costs from permit prices, but border fees on comparable imports and rebates for exporters are designed to leave them competitive, so the bill deliberately shields them from losing to countries without carbon rules.
